1387.title: Rejecting extremism
1387.hook: scholars have condemned terrorism as against Islam, as in the Open Letter to al-Baghdadi
1387.howItsDone: Muslim scholars and organizations issue public letters, fatwas and declarations against terrorism, often arguing from the Qur'an and hadith point by point, and imams address the subject in sermons.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Islamic finance, trade permitted, riba forbidden, and an honest argument about the difference. Your line was finance without interest. Today, a harder question, and a new week.

The letter is addressed to one man, by name: Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, who had declared himself caliph of the group called ISIS, and to the fighters who followed him. Not to the world, not to the press. It's written in Arabic, in the language of the law he claimed to be applying, and signed by Muslim scholars and leaders from many countries. Its message, point after point, is a single word: no.
screen: `ADDRESSED TO ONE MAN.` → `WRITTEN IN HIS OWN TERMS.` → `ONE WORD: NO.`

segments.voice: The Open Letter to al-Baghdadi doesn't shout. It argues, verse by verse, like a teacher marking an exam. Issuing religious rulings without the learning they require is forbidden. Killing the innocent is forbidden. Killing emissaries is forbidden, and so killing journalists and aid workers is too. Torture is forbidden. Declaring other Muslims to be unbelievers, when they haven't declared it themselves, is forbidden. And fighting in Islam has rules, a right cause and a right conduct, and isn't permitted without them. Behind those points sit texts anyone can read. In Surah al-Baqarah, Pickthall: "Fight in the way of Allah against those who fight against you, but begin not hostilities. Lo! Allah loveth not aggressors." And in Sunan an-Nasa'i the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, warns against going to extremes in religion, saying, in paraphrase, that people before you were destroyed by it. The Arabic word is ghuluw: overshooting, going past the mark. Read beside the letter, the hadith names the charge. Not too much religion. Excess that leaves religion behind. And the letter is one statement among several. Scholars in different countries have issued their own fatwas and declarations against terrorism, in mosques and in print, public for anyone to read. They say, in their own words, what today's line says in three.
screen: `AN ARGUMENT, POINT BY POINT.` · `BEGIN NOT HOSTILITIES.` · `GHULUW: GOING PAST THE MARK.` · `SIGNED, DATED, AND PUBLIC.`

If you pray, pray for those harmed in that faith's name; if you don't, simply hold them in mind.

Your line: scholars said no. Point by point, in their own terms and texts. Until tomorrow.

1388.title: Killing innocents
1388.hook: the Qur'an: whoever kills a soul unjustly, it's as if he killed all humanity (5:32)
1388.howItsDone: Muslim scholars and preachers cite 5:32 when condemning attacks on civilians, and some mosques hold prayers for victims of violence, whoever they are.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rejecting extremism, and a letter that answered a self-declared caliph point by point. Your line was scholars said no. Today, the verse underneath that no.

Two brothers, the sons of Adam, each bring an offering. One is accepted, one isn't. The one refused says, I will kill you. The other answers, in the Qur'an's telling, that even if his brother reaches out a hand to kill him, he won't reach out his own. Then it happens anyway. The killer doesn't even know what to do with the body, until a raven scratches at the ground and shows him. That's Surah al-Ma'idah. Straight after the grave comes the verse.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS, TWO OFFERINGS.` → `I WON'T RAISE MY HAND.` → `A RAVEN AND A GRAVE.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall: "whosoever killeth a human being for other than manslaughter or corruption in the earth, it shall be as if he had killed all mankind, and whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind." Three things in that sentence. First, who. The Arabic word is nafs, a soul, a living person. Not a believer, not a neighbor, not one of us. A human being. Second, the arithmetic. One death counts as all of humanity. The verse refuses to let a single killing be small. And it runs the other way: save one life, and it's as if you saved everyone. A paramedic, a lifeguard, a stranger who pulls someone back from the curb. Third, where it's set. The verse begins, for that cause, We decreed for the Children of Israel. Placed right after the story of Adam's two sons, and given as a decree to an earlier people, it reaches back before Islam, to the family of Adam. The hadith then draw lines even inside war. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn 'Umar reports that a woman was found killed after one of the Prophet's battles, and the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, forbade the killing of women and children. And in the Muwatta of Imam Malik, Abu Bakr sends an army out with orders: do not kill women, or children, or the old; do not cut down fruit trees. Even in war, there were lines.
screen: `NAFS: A HUMAN BEING, ANY HUMAN BEING.` · `ONE LIFE COUNTS AS ALL.` · `SET AFTER ADAM'S TWO SONS.` · `EVEN IN WAR, LINES.`

Hold them as a whole world, the way the verse counts them. If you pray, pray for them and those who grieve them, in your own words or the ones you usually use; if not, simply keep them in mind.
Killing innocents. In Surah al-Ma'idah, to kill one human being unjustly is as if killing all mankind; to save one is as if saving all. Today's word.
Your line: every soul sacred. No one is only a number. Go gently.

1389.title: Interfaith friendship
1389.hook: A Common Word, a Muslim letter to Christian leaders on love of God and neighbor
1389.howItsDone: Muslims take part in interfaith dialogue through letters like A Common Word, mosque open days, shared meals and community service with churches and synagogues, and some point to 3:64 and 49:13 when they explain why.

segments.voice: Yesterday: killing innocents, the verse that counts one life as all mankind. Your line was every soul sacred. Today, from a stranger's worth to a friendship.

"Come to an agreement between us and you." That's a line from the Qur'an, and it became the title of a letter. Not a treaty or a press release: a long, careful letter from Muslim scholars, addressed to Christian leaders by name, the Pope among them, along with the heads of churches East and West. It doesn't ask anyone to change their faith. It asks them to look at two commandments both sides already say out loud.
screen: `A LINE BECOMES A TITLE.` → `ADDRESSED BY NAME.` → `TWO COMMANDMENTS.`

segments.voice: Start with the verse the title comes from, Surah Al 'Imran, in Pickthall: "Say: O People of the Scripture! Come to an agreement between us and you." People of the Scripture is the Qur'an's name for Jews and Christians. The Arabic for that agreement is kalimatin sawa', a word held in common, level between two parties. The letter asks: what word do we already share? Its answer is two loves: love of God, and love of neighbor. On the Christian side, it quotes Jesus from the Gospel of Mark, in the King James words: "thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart," and "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." On the Muslim side it sets the Qur'an's call to love and remember God next to a hadith in Sahih Muslim, where the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase, that none of you truly believes until he loves for his neighbor what he loves for himself. Notice what the letter doesn't do. It doesn't say the two faiths are the same, or ask anyone to agree on who Jesus is. It says: here is ground we both already stand on, so let's meet there, and live in peace. Some Muslims set another verse beside it, from Surah al-Hujurat: "We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Know one another. Not merge, not argue anyone out of anything. Letters like this can sound lofty, but the word at the center of this one is the plainest there is: neighbor.
screen: `COME TO AN AGREEMENT.` · `LOVE OF GOD, LOVE OF NEIGHBOR.` · `COMMON GROUND, NOT SAMENESS.` · `THAT YE MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you know whose faith, or lack of one, differs from yours, a coworker, a neighbor, a classmate's parent, and see their face. Ask yourself what you actually know about what matters to them, and find one honest, friendly question you could ask. If you pray, hold them in mind as a neighbor; if you don't, simply hold the question.

1390.title: Facing Islamophobia
1390.hook: prejudice against Muslims, and how communities respond with patience and openness
1390.howItsDone: Muslim communities facing prejudice respond in different ways: some mosques hold open days and invite neighbors in, while community groups also document incidents, support those targeted, and work with the police and the courts.

segments.voice: Yesterday: interfaith friendship, and a letter built on two commandments. Your line was love of God and neighbor. Today, the neighbor who doesn't want to know you.

A note taped to a mosque door overnight. Ugly words, misspelled, telling the people inside to go home, when this is home. The imam finds it before dawn prayer. What happens next is a choice. Some mosques that have faced moments like this have answered by opening the doors wider: an open day, tea in the hall, a sign that says come in and ask us anything. It isn't the only answer, and it isn't easy.
screen: `A NOTE ON THE DOOR.` → `WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?` → `THE DOORS OPEN WIDER.`

segments.voice: Islamophobia is the word people use for prejudice and hostility toward Muslims, and toward people taken to be Muslim because of a name, a beard or a headscarf. It can be a shout on a bus, a vandalized wall, or a door that quietly stays closed at a job interview. The tradition has its own memory of rejection. In Sahih al-Bukhari, 'A'ishah asks the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, whether he ever had a day harder than the battle of Uhud. He says yes: a day he went to a man of standing to ask for support, and was turned away. He walked off so grieved, he says, that he hardly knew where he was until he reached a place on the road. Then an angel of the mountains came and offered to bring the two mountains down on the town. And he said no. He hoped, instead, that from their descendants would come people who worship God alone. The Qur'an puts the principle in Surah Fussilat, in Pickthall: "Repel the evil deed with one which is better." The one who was your enemy, it goes on, may become like a close friend. In Surah al-Furqan, the servants of the Merciful answer the ignorant who address them with: peace. But patience isn't the same as silence. Communities also document what happens, report it, and turn to the law. The Prophet's answer that day wasn't to pretend nothing had happened. It was to refuse to answer in kind, and keep a future open.
screen: `PREJUDICE TOWARD MUSLIMS.` · `THE HARDEST DAY: TURNED AWAY.` · `REPEL THE EVIL DEED WITH A BETTER ONE.` · `PATIENCE IS NOT SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Picture a train, a store, a sidewalk, where someone is being shouted at for how they look or pray. You don't confront the shouter: you walk over, stand beside the person targeted, say something ordinary, hi, are you okay, want to walk with me, and stay until it's over, then ask what they need. If you pray, hold that person in mind; if you don't, rehearse that first sentence until it's yours.
Facing Islamophobia. Prejudice against Muslims, met with patience, openness, and the refusal to answer in kind. Today's word.
Your line: answer hate with good. Patience, and a future kept open. That's today, done.

1391.title: Mental health and faith
1391.hook: Muslim voices encouraging therapy alongside prayer
1391.howItsDone: Some imams now refer people to counselors, and Muslim therapists and support lines offer care that makes room for prayer and faith alongside treatment.

segments.voice: Yesterday: facing Islamophobia, a prophet who refused to answer in kind. Your line was answer hate with good. Today goes deeper into day one hundred thirty-one: the heavy heart, the du'a and the doctor.

If I need a therapist, does that mean my faith is weak? Some imams hear that after the prayer, quietly, by the shoe racks, and some now answer: pray, yes, and also see someone. Some Muslim counselors and therapists work with both in the room, the prayer mat and the treatment plan. The question underneath is old: can a person of deep faith be crushed by sorrow? The Qur'an answers with a father, and a son he thought he'd lost.
screen: `DOES IT MEAN MY FAITH IS WEAK?` → `PRAY, AND SEE SOMEONE.` → `A FATHER AND A LOST SON.`

segments.voice: In Surah Yusuf, the prophet Ya'qub loses his beloved son Yusuf, and later another son too. He turns away from the others, the surah says, and his eyes go white with sorrow. His sons tell him he'll grieve himself to death. He answers, in paraphrase, that he lays out his distress and his grief to Allah alone. He is a prophet, and he is not okay. The Qur'an doesn't hide his grief or call it a failure. And he names it, out loud, to God. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, wept too. In Sahih al-Bukhari, when his infant son Ibrahim was dying, his eyes filled with tears; when a companion was surprised, he said, in paraphrase: the eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. Then a short report in Jami' at-Tirmidhi. A man asks whether he should tie up his camel and trust in God, or leave it loose and trust. The answer: tie it, and trust. Trust is not instead of action. Prayer is not instead of care. So when someone with depression keeps both their prayers and their therapy appointment, some Muslim counselors would say they're tying the camel. The Arabic word for heart is qalb, and the Qur'an speaks of hearts that are sick and hearts that find rest. In that reading, healing it two ways isn't doubting God. And said plainly: if the heaviness is taking your sleep or your hope, or you've thought about not being here, please reach for help today. In the US, call or text 988; elsewhere, local emergency help.
screen: `YA'QUB: MY DISTRESS, UNTO ALLAH.` · `THE EYES SHED TEARS, THE HEART GRIEVES.` · `TIE YOUR CAMEL, AND TRUST.` · `PRAYER AND CARE, TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself honestly how your heart is today, in a real word: tired, heavy, restless, light. 1392.title: Technology and worship
1392.hook: prayer apps, online Qur'an, and the need for real presence
1392.howItsDone: Muslims today may use apps or printed timetables for prayer times and the direction of the qibla, and some put the phone on silent or in another room before they pray.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mental health and faith, prayer and therapy side by side. Your line was heal the heart two ways. Today, the thing in your pocket.

The app chimes. 'Asr, it says, and a little compass on the screen swings around to point toward Mecca. The mat goes down, the phone beside it, face up, and the prayer begins. Second rak'ah, forehead on the floor, and the screen lights up: a name, half a message. The prayer carries on. The mind doesn't, quite. What does a phone in the pocket do to a prayer? An old report in al-Bukhari fits.
screen: `THE APP CHIMES FOR 'ASR.` → `THE SCREEN LIGHTS UP MID-PRAYER.` → `AN OLD REPORT FOR A NEW MOMENT.`

segments.voice: The report is told by 'Aisha. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, once prayed in a garment with markings on it, a patterned cloth, and during the prayer his eye caught the pattern. When he finished he said, in paraphrase: take this to Abu Jahm and bring me his plain one, because this one just distracted me in my prayer. Right beside it, al-Bukhari keeps a second report, about a curtain with pictures hanging in 'Aisha's house. The Prophet asked for it to be taken down, because its pictures kept coming to him while he prayed. He didn't give up clothes, or curtains. He swapped the one thing that kept pulling at his attention for something plain. The tool stayed. The distraction went. The Qur'an has a word for what was being protected. The chapter called The Believers opens, in Pickthall's translation: "Successful indeed are the believers / Who are humble in their prayers." Muslim teachers call that humility in prayer khushu': stillness, lowered eyes, the whole person turned one way. And in the conversation with the angel Gabriel, the Prophet describes ihsan, doing a thing beautifully, in paraphrase: to worship Allah as though you see Him, and though you don't see Him, He sees you. That is presence. So the question about technology is an old one. An app that tells you when Maghrib comes is a timetable. A screen that shows the Qur'an is a page. Both can serve the prayer. 'Aisha's report asks something simpler and harder: what keeps coming to you while you pray, and can you hand it to Abu Jahm?
screen: `A PATTERNED GARMENT, HANDED BACK.` · `A CURTAIN TAKEN DOWN.` · `THE TOOL STAYS. THE DISTRACTION GOES.` · `KHUSHU': THE WHOLE PERSON TURNED ONE WAY.` · then, large: `AS THOUGH YOU SEE HIM.`

segments.voice: Set the phone in another room, or face down out of reach, and notice any pull toward it, an itch to check; don't fight it, just notice it, the way the Prophet noticed the pattern on the cloth. Then let your attention come back to one thing: your breath, the room around you, or, if you pray, al-Fatiha said slowly in your head. When the pull comes again, notice it, and come back again.
Technology and worship. Apps, screens and timetables that can serve a prayer, and the presence that no tool can supply. Today's word.
Your line: real presence. The tool stays; the distraction goes. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1393.title: Social media and the tongue
1393.hook: the adab of speech applies online too
1393.howItsDone: Some Muslim teachers apply the hadith on speech, say good or keep silent, to messaging and social media, and some Muslims make a habit of checking a story before they share it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: technology and worship, and a patterned garment handed back. Your line was real presence. Today, what the thumbs say.

Does backbiting count if you type it instead of saying it? Does passing on a rumor count if all you did was tap share? Does a cruel comment under a stranger's photo count, if the stranger never reads it? The sayings about speech come from a world of rooms, doorways and roads, where a listener usually stood in front of the speaker. Now a word can reach a crowd of screens before its writer has put the phone down. Today takes the old manners of the tongue, what Muslims call adab, and carries them online.
screen: `DOES IT COUNT IF YOU TYPE IT?` → `WORDS ONCE HAD A FACE IN FRONT OF THEM.` → `THE ADAB OF SPEECH, ONLINE.`

segments.voice: Start with the plainest rule. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say what is good, or keep silent. Good, or nothing. There's no third box marked technically true but unkind. Then a second report, also in al-Bukhari: a Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand other Muslims are safe. Tongue and hand, side by side. On a phone, the hand does the talking. The thumbs are the tongue. Third, the rumor. Imam Muslim, in the introduction to his collection, keeps a saying that it is enough of a lie for a person to pass on everything he hears. Not inventing anything. Just passing it on. And the Qur'an, in the chapter called The Private Apartments, asks the believers to check a report brought by someone untrustworthy before acting on it, so they don't harm people in ignorance and regret it afterward. A few verses later, the same chapter forbids backbiting, and asks, in a picture that's hard to forget, whether any of you would love to eat the flesh of a dead brother. Hold the four up to a screen. Say good or stay quiet. Let your hand be as safe as your tongue. Don't pass on everything that reaches you. Check it before you act on it. None of these rules mentions a phone, and every one of them fits on one.
screen: `SAY GOOD, OR KEEP SILENT.` · `THE TONGUE AND THE HAND, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `DON'T PASS ON EVERYTHING YOU HEAR.` · `CHECK THE REPORT FIRST.` · then, large: `THE THUMBS ARE THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last few things you typed to anyone, a message, a comment, a post, and let them come up one at a time without judging. For each, ask the hadith's question: was it good, or would silence have been better? If one stings a little, notice it and let it go with the breath; if you pray, you can ask for a careful tongue.
Social media and the tongue. The old manners of speech, say good or stay silent, check before you pass it on, carried into every post and comment. Today's word.
